newsitem.title: USA: U.S. astronauts begin Hubble upgrade.
newsitem.headline: U.S. astronauts begin Hubble upgrade.

text.p: Two spacewalking astronauts from shuttle Discovery eased two new scientific instruments into the Hubble Space Telescope on Friday, starting a $350 million orbital tune-up.
Mark Lee and Steve Smith gently removed two of the telescope's ageing instruments and replaced them with an improved light-splitting spectrograph and a multipurpose infrared camera.

The installation of the state-of-the-art-spectrograph called STIS was the first item on the astronauts' list of 10 upgrades for the orbiting observatory. The $125 million instrument will aid astronomers seeking massive black holes.
It proved a little tricky to fit the 700 lb (320 kg), refrigerator-sized spectrograph precisely inside the telescope, but the work was completed on time.
"Nice job on that you guys," said astronaut Joe Tanner, who monitored the spacewalk from the shuttle's cabin. "It was a lot harder than we thought."
An initial test of the instrument showed it was working properly, and the astronauts then turned their attention toward installing a $105 million infrared camera, known as NICMOS.

The camera's detectors, cooled to -355 degrees Fahrenheit (-215 Celsius) by a block of frozen nitrogen, will allow astronomers to see deeper into the universe and peer through veils of dust to see newborn stars. Scientists hoped the instrument would also take the first images of planets orbiting distant stars.
Lee and Smith, wearing bulky white spacesuits, began the spacewalk at about 11:45 p.m. EST on Thursday (0445 GMT on Friday) as the shuttle soared 360 miles (575 km) above Australia.
"Oh my gosh, beautiful," said Smith as he floated outside with the gleaming, silver observatory towering overhead. "Wow, look at that telescope," added Lee.
Smith worked perched on the end of the shuttle's 50-foot (15-meter) robot arm, while Lee floated free, often completely inside the telescope.
The start of the spacewalk was held up for one hour and 45 minutes after one of the telescope's two fragile solar arrays swung round violently and unexpectedly.

"We saw something real unusual," Tanner radioed mission control. "The ... array skewed from horizontal to vertical and then about halfway back to horizontal." The rapid movement of the 40-ft (12-metre)-long panel occurred in just five seconds, he said.
"That must have been very dramatic," mission control's Jeff Hoffman replied.

Lee and Smith were about to leave the shuttle's airlock when the incident occurred. Flight controllers said air vented into space from the airlock compartment had struck the panel and set it moving. The delicate array appeared unharmed by the incident, they said.

Three more spacewalks were planned to complete the refurbishment of the telescope. Other upgrades included the installation of a new digital tape recorder, a more accurate guidance sensor for pointing the telescope and various improved electronic boxes.
It was the first time astronauts had worked on the $2 billion orbiting observatory since the 1993 repair that fixed its blurred vision.
